61.tq: Combine route and outcome to reject the permanent-annexation trap.

61.s: Samudragupta celebrated his conquests by performing which ritual?
61.x: Samudragupta performed an Ashvamedha to celebrate his military achievements and also issued Ashvamedha coins.
61.tq: Match the ruler’s conquest celebration with the specific Vedic ritual.

61.s: Which of the following features is represented on some coins of Samudragupta?
o: The ruler performing a fire sacrifice with a tiger
The ruler receiving tribute from a Roman ambassador
The ruler riding an elephant with a bow
61.x: Some coins of Samudragupta depict him playing the veena, reflecting his association with music and culture.
61.tq: Use the distinctive coin-type image rather than a general military association.

61.s: Who among the following is mentioned as a minister of Samudragupta?
61.x: The Buddhist scholar Vasubandhu is mentioned as a minister of Samudragupta. Harisena was his court poet and author of the Allahabad Prasasti.
61.tq: Distinguish the minister from the court poet and other Gupta-era literary figures.

61.s: The Allahabad Prasasti is composed in which language?
61.x: The Allahabad or Prayaga Prasasti is a Sanskrit eulogy of Samudragupta’s conquests.
61.tq: Test the language of the inscription against the major literary languages of ancient India.

61.s: The Allahabad Prasasti is written in which literary form?
o: Mixed prose and verse in champu style
A copper-plate grant in formal legal prose
61.x: The Prasasti combines prose and verse and is composed in the champu style.
61.tq: Identify the exact literary form rather than merely the language of the inscription.

61.s: Which of the following offices was NOT held by Harisena?
61.x: Harisena held the offices of Kumaramatya, Sandhivigrahika and Mahadandanayaka. He was not a Mahamatra of Ashoka, who belonged to an earlier period.
61.tq: Reject the office belonging to another imperial administrative system.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about Harisena:
1. He was associated with the court of Samudragupta.
2. He held the offices of Kumaramatya, Sandhivigrahika and Mahadandanayaka.
3. He should be identified without distinction with the later Jain author of the Brihatkatha Kosha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Harisena associated with Samudragupta must not be confused with the later Jain author of the Brihatkatha Kosha.
61.tq: Use the confusable-person trap and separate two authors with the same name.

61.s: Which of the following inscriptions is found on the same pillar that bears the Allahabad Prasasti?
61.x: The pillar bearing the Allahabad Prasasti also carries an inscription of Jahangir, along with Ashoka’s edicts and the Queen’s edict.
61.tq: Identify the inscription by location and avoid confusing separate monuments.

61.s: The Queen’s edict on the pillar bearing the Allahabad Prasasti is associated with:
61.x: The Queen’s edict on the pillar is associated with Queen Karuvaki.
61.tq: Link the specific edict with its named queen rather than with Gupta royal women.

61.s: Which of the following correctly contrasts the messages associated with the inscriptions on the Allahabad pillar?
o: The Allahabad Prasasti glorifies war, whereas Ashoka’s message on the same pillar emphasises peace.
The Allahabad Prasasti advocates Buddhism, whereas Ashoka’s edicts glorify military conquest.
Both the Allahabad Prasasti and Ashoka’s edicts reject warfare in identical terms.
Both inscriptions are primarily commercial records concerning trade routes.
61.x: The Allahabad Prasasti celebrates Samudragupta’s military conquests, while Ashoka’s inscriptions on the same pillar convey a message associated with peace and dhamma.
61.tq: Use the reversed-comparison trap to distinguish the tone and purpose of the two inscriptions.

61.s: Which of the following records is associated with the Samudragupta period in the Andhra region?
o: The Amaravati record of Gautamiputra Satakarni
The Motupalli charter of the Kakatiyas
61.x: A record belonging to the Samudragupta period is noted at Sankaram in the Visakhapatnam region.
61.tq: Use the regional location clue to identify the relevant inscriptional record.

61.s: Which Gupta ruler is regarded as the real founder of the Gupta Empire and ruled approximately from 319 to 335 CE?
61.x: Chandragupta I, who ruled approximately from 319 to 335 CE, is regarded as the real founder of the Gupta Empire.
61.tq: Use direct ruler-identification from the title or role associated with the ruler.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about the territorial base of Chandragupta I:
1. His authority extended over South Bihar.
2. Saketa and Prayaga formed part of his dominions.
3. Pataliputra was his capital.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Chandragupta I ruled South Bihar and parts of eastern Uttar Pradesh, including Saketa and Prayaga, with Pataliputra as his capital.
61.tq: Combine territorial, capital and administrative facts, checking whether all statements belong to the same ruler.

61.s: The marriage of Chandragupta I with Kumaradevi was significant primarily because it:
o: secured control over the western seaboard
gave the Guptas legitimacy and political strength through the Lichchhavis
ended the Gupta conflict with the Sakas
established matrimonial relations with the Vakatakas
61.x: Kumaradevi was a Lichchhavi princess, and the marriage enhanced Gupta legitimacy, prestige and political power.
61.tq: Identify the political consequence of a dynastic marriage rather than merely recalling the name.

61.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
61.x: Kumaradevi was the queen of Chandragupta I. Duttadevi, Kuberanaga and Anantadevi were associated with Samudragupta, Chandragupta II and Kumaragupta I respectively.
61.tq: Use king–queen association and eliminate the swapped matrimonial pairs.

61.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (King)
A. Chandragupta I
B. Samudragupta
C. Chandragupta II
D. Kumaragupta I

List-II (Queen)
1. Anantadevi
2. Kumaradevi
3. Duttadevi
4. Kuberanaga

Which of the following is correct?
61.x: Chandragupta I–Kumaradevi, Samudragupta–Duttadevi, Chandragupta II–Kuberanaga and Kumaragupta I–Anantadevi are the correct pairs.
61.tq: Start with the sure king–queen pair and eliminate codes containing a swapped pair.

61.s: Which of the following statements regarding Gupta matrimonial links is NOT correctly matched?
61.x: Dhruvadevi was associated first with Ramagupta and subsequently with Chandragupta II; therefore the pair presenting Ramagupta alone with the relationship is incomplete and is not correctly matched. Chandragupta II married Kuberanaga, while Prabhavati Gupta was married to Rudrasena II.
61.tq: Find the option that distorts a linked sequence rather than simply swapping two names.

61.s: The early Gupta gold coins showing Chandragupta I and Kumaradevi are generally known as the:
61.x: The first Gupta gold coins issued by Chandragupta I are the King-Queen type, depicting Chandragupta I and Kumaradevi in association with the Lichchhavis.
61.tq: Distinguish coin types by the figures represented on them.

61.s: Which one of the following is the correct sequence in the early Gupta line?
61.x: The early Gupta succession is Sri Gupta, followed by Ghatotkacha, and then Chandragupta I.
61.tq: Fix the first and last rulers before checking the middle succession.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about the origin of the Guptas:
1. Their origin is regarded as certain and undisputed.
2. They rose from relatively modest beginnings.
3. Their caste identity has been debated.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: The origin of the Guptas is uncertain and debated. They rose from modest beginnings, and their caste identity has also been disputed.
61.tq: Reject the absolute statement when the historical issue is expressly described as debated.

61.s: Which one of the following statements best reflects the debate regarding the caste origin of the Guptas?
o: They were exclusively Shudras according to all inscriptions.
Their caste origin is established by the Junagadh inscription.
They were universally accepted as Kshatriyas from the beginning.
They were originally Vaishyas, later treated by Brahmanas as Kshatriyas; a Brahmana origin has also been argued.
61.x: The Guptas are described as originally Vaishyas who were later treated as Kshatriyas by Brahmanas; a Brahmana origin has also been proposed on the basis of the Dharana gotra.
61.tq: Separate the commonly stated view from an alternative scholarly argument instead of treating one claim as conclusive.

61.s: Sri Gupta is associated with which of the following regions as his early sphere of authority?
61.x: Sri Gupta is stated to have ruled a small part of North Bengal and South Bihar.
61.tq: Use precise geographical discrimination among nearby historical regions.

61.s: The earliest Gupta political territory is described as comprising primarily:
o: Magadha, Prayaga and eastern Uttar Pradesh
61.x: The early Gupta territory was centred on Magadha, Prayaga and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
61.tq: Match the dynasty’s formative territorial core rather than its later expansion.

61.s: Which inscription provides evidence regarding Chandragupta II's conquests in the north-west and Bengal?
61.x: The Mehrauli iron pillar inscription is associated with Chandragupta II and refers to his conquests in the north-west and Bengal.
61.tq: Use the ruler–inscription association to distinguish similar Gupta epigraphic sources.

61.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Eran inscription — Governors called Lokapala
2. Bhitari pillar — Defeat of the Hunas
3. Junagadh inscription — Repair of the Sudarshana lake
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
61.x: The Eran source refers to governors called Lokapala, the Bhitari pillar records Skandagupta's defeat of the Hunas, and the Junagadh inscription records the repair of the Sudarshana lake.
61.tq: Verify each source–content pair independently before selecting the coded combination.

61.s: Who was the governor responsible for repairing the Sudarshana lake during the reign of Skandagupta?
61.x: Parnadatta, the governor of Skandagupta, was responsible for the repair of the Sudarshana lake, as recorded in the Junagadh inscription.
61.tq: Identify the official connected with a public work rather than the ruler named in the inscription.

61.s: The Eran inscription of the Gupta period is associated with which of the following statements?
o: It refers to governors designated as Lokapala.
It records the Sri Lankan request for a monastery at Bodh Gaya.
It describes Chandragupta II's western conquests.
61.x: The Eran inscription is associated with Samudragupta and refers to governors called Lokapala.
61.tq: Eliminate options belonging to other inscriptions, literary works or diplomatic records.

61.s: The work Devichandraguptam, attributed to Vishakhadatta, deals with the episode involving:
61.x: Devichandraguptam narrates the episode involving Ramagupta, Dhruvadevi and Chandragupta II.
61.tq: Match a literary work with its distinctive dramatis personae.

61.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Mudrarakshasa — Political drama concerning Chanakya and Chandragupta Maurya
61.x: Mudrarakshasa, written by Vishakhadatta, is a political drama concerning Chanakya and Chandragupta Maurya. Devichandraguptam is also associated with Vishakhadatta, while the Prayaga Prasasti was composed by Harishena.
61.tq: Use author–work–subject combinations and reject cross-linked distractors.

61.s: Which of the following literary sources is particularly useful for information about the early territorial extent of the Gupta Empire?
61.x: The Puranas, including the Vayu Purana, describe the early Gupta territory.
61.tq: Distinguish a geographical source from literary works dealing with political drama or statecraft.

61.s:
Gupta coins are important historical sources because they provide evidence about:
1. Royal titles
2. Religious affiliations
3. Ritual practices and prosperity
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Gupta coins, mostly gold, depict rulers, deities and rituals and thereby reveal royal titles, religious ideas, ritual practices and the prosperity of the period.
61.tq: Recognise the multiple kinds of historical information conveyed by coin evidence.

61.s: Which ruler sent an embassy to Samudragupta seeking permission to build a monastery and a rest house at Bodh Gaya?
61.x: Meghavarman, the Buddhist ruler of Sri Lanka, sent a mission to Samudragupta for permission to build a monastery and rest house at Bodh Gaya.
61.tq: Identify the foreign ruler and the diplomatic purpose together.

61.s: The embassy of Meghavarman to the Gupta court is known primarily through:
61.x: The mission of Meghavarman and the request concerning Bodh Gaya are recorded in a Chinese source.
61.tq: Separate the event from the different types of sources used to record it.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about Gupta foreign relations:
1. Kushanas and Sakas paid homage to the Gupta ruler.
2. Kings of Southeast Asia and Ceylon sent tribute.
3. Gupta foreign contacts were confined entirely to northern India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Kushanas and Sakas paid homage, while rulers of Southeast Asia and Ceylon sent tribute. Gupta foreign contacts were not confined entirely to northern India.
61.tq: Spot the geographically extreme statement that conflicts with the wider diplomatic evidence.

61.s: Which of the following statements about Chandragupta II's external commercial links is correct?
o: His trade was restricted to the Himalayan region.
His trade routes bypassed the western sea entirely.
His sea trade reached Europe through Egypt.
His maritime contacts were limited to Sri Lanka alone.
61.x: Chandragupta II's sea trade reached Europe via Egypt, indicating wide-ranging maritime commercial contacts.
61.tq: Use the route detail to distinguish a precise trade statement from restrictive distractors.

61.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Fa-Hien is correct?
o: He visited India during Samudragupta's reign and described the Allahabad inscription.
He was an ambassador sent by Meghavarman of Sri Lanka.
He explicitly names Chandragupta II as the ruler under whom he travelled.
He travelled in the empire of Chandragupta II but did not name the king.
61.x: Fa-Hien travelled in the empire of Chandragupta II, but his account does not name the king directly.
61.tq: Distinguish the period identified through historical reconstruction from the name explicitly mentioned by the traveller.

61.s: Which type of Samudragupta's coinage portrays him as a poet and musician?
61.x: The lyrist or veena-player type depicts Samudragupta as a poet-musician and supports the association of the title Kaviraja with him.
61.tq: Match a coin type with the distinctive activity depicted on it.

61.s: The Ashvamedha type of Samudragupta's coins was issued after he:
o: received the embassy from Sri Lanka
61.x: Samudragupta issued the Ashvamedha type after performing the Ashvamedha, or horse sacrifice.
61.tq: Connect a commemorative coin type with the event it celebrates.

61.s: Which of the following is NOT a type of coin attributed to Samudragupta?
61.x: The King-Queen type belongs to the coinage of Chandragupta I, whereas Samudragupta issued lyrist, Ashvamedha and archer types among others.
61.tq: Identify the coin type belonging to a different ruler.

61.s: Which one of the following sets contains only coin types associated with Samudragupta?
61.x: Lyrist, Ashvamedha and archer are all types of Samudragupta's coinage. The King-Queen type belongs to Chandragupta I, while the other options combine unrelated descriptions.
61.tq: Test the whole set and reject options containing a coin type of another ruler.

61.s: Who composed the Allahabad Pillar inscription, also known as the Prayaga Prashasti, of Samudragupta?
61.x: Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta, composed the Allahabad Pillar inscription in Sanskrit on an Ashokan pillar.
61.tq: Use the composer–ruler association to distinguish similar Gupta inscriptions.

61.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Mehrauli Iron Pillar — Chandragupta II
2. Udayagiri cave inscription — Virasena
3. Bhitari inscription — Skandagupta
4. Mandsaur inscription — Vatsabhatti
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
61.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. The Mehrauli pillar refers to ‘Chandra’, identified with Chandragupta II; Virasena was connected with Udayagiri, Vatsabhatti with Mandsaur, and the Bhitari inscription belongs to Skandagupta.
61.tq: Test several inscription–ruler or composer pairs together and eliminate through the surest pair.

61.s: Which one of the following inscriptions is associated with the record of Bhanugupta dated to 510 CE?
61.x: The later record at Eran belongs to Bhanugupta and is dated to 510 CE.
61.tq: Identify the inscription through its ruler and date rather than through a famous monument.

61.s: The earliest evidence of sati among the inscriptions listed below is provided by the record of
61.x: Bhanugupta’s record at Eran is described as the earliest evidence of sati among the listed records.
61.tq: Distinguish two records from the same site by matching the later ruler with the special historical evidence.

61.s: The Mandsaur inscription is associated with which one of the following combinations?
o: Kumaragupta I, feudatory Bandhuvarman and Vatsabhatti
Chandragupta II, Rudrasimha III and Kalidasa
61.x: The Mandsaur record belongs to the period of Kumaragupta I, under the feudatory Bandhuvarman, and was composed by Vatsabhatti. It also refers to a guild of silk-weavers.
61.tq: Start from the distinctive composer–inscription pair and verify the associated ruler.

61.s: The Bhitari inscription is particularly associated with which achievement of the Gupta ruler concerned?
61.x: The Bhitari inscription of Skandagupta records the repulse of the Hunas.
61.tq: Match the inscription with the specific military achievement instead of its location alone.

61.s: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the early Gupta rulers?
o: Ghatotkacha, Sri Gupta, Chandragupta I, Samudragupta
Sri Gupta, Ghatotkacha, Chandragupta I, Samudragupta
Sri Gupta, Chandragupta I, Ghatotkacha, Samudragupta
Chandragupta I, Sri Gupta, Ghatotkacha, Samudragupta
61.x: Sri Gupta was followed by Ghatotkacha, Chandragupta I and Samudragupta.
61.tq: Fix the founder as the first item and then arrange the successive rulers.

61.s: Which Gupta ruler is generally regarded as the founder of the Gupta dynasty and is dated approximately to 240–280 CE?
61.x: Sri Gupta is identified as the founder of the Gupta dynasty and is assigned approximately to 240–280 CE.
61.tq: Link the founder with the earliest date range rather than with the better-known imperial rulers.

61.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
61.x: Samudragupta ruled approximately from 335 to 375 CE. Ghatotkacha belonged to c. 280–319 CE, Chandragupta I to 319–335 CE, and Chandragupta II to about 380–413 CE.
61.tq: Compare adjacent Gupta date ranges and reject shifted reign periods.

61.s:
Arrange the following Gupta rulers in chronological order:
A. Kumaragupta I
B. Ramagupta
C. Skandagupta
D. Chandragupta II
61.x: The order is Ramagupta, Chandragupta II, Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta. Ramagupta’s reign was brief, while Chandragupta II preceded Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta.
61.tq: Place the less firmly dated brief reign first, then use the established succession.

61.s: The approximate reign of Skandagupta was
61.x: Skandagupta ruled approximately from 455 to 467 CE.
61.tq: Use the ruler’s position at the end of the listed Gupta succession to identify the latest date range.

61.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Chandragupta II’s western conquests is correct?
o: He defeated Bhanugupta and annexed Bengal.
He defeated Bandhuvarman and annexed coastal Andhra.
He defeated Rudrasimha III and annexed western Malwa and Gujarat.
He defeated Hastivarman and annexed Kanchi.
61.x: Chandragupta II defeated the Saka ruler Rudrasimha III and annexed western Malwa and Gujarat, thereby reaching the western sea.
61.tq: Use the ruler–opponent–territory combination to avoid swapped military achievements.

61.s: Chandragupta II issued silver coins on the Saka model primarily because he
o: established Ujjain as the first Gupta capital
imitated the coins of the Vakatakas
replaced all Gupta gold coins with silver coins
introduced a new currency for the conquered western region
61.x: After acquiring the western region, Chandragupta II issued silver coins on the Saka model for the new territory.
61.tq: Connect a monetary change with the administrative needs of a newly conquered region.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about Chandragupta II:
1. He married the Naga princess Kuberanaga.
2. His daughter Prabhavati Gupta married Vakataka Rudrasena II.
3. The marriage alliance helped extend Gupta influence into the Deccan.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: All three statements are correct. Chandragupta II married Kuberanaga, while Prabhavati Gupta married Rudrasena II of the Vakatakas, providing indirect Gupta control in the Deccan.
61.tq: Treat marriage alliances as political relationships and verify all linked statements.

61.s: Which city was made the second capital by Chandragupta II?
61.x: Chandragupta II made Ujjain his second capital.
61.tq: Discriminate between a political capital and places associated with inscriptions or conquests.

61.s: The coins of Chandragupta II depicting him killing a lion are contrasted with the coins of his father, which depicted him killing a
61.x: Chandragupta II is associated with lion-slayer coins, whereas his father is associated with tiger-slayer coins.
61.tq: Separate similar coin types through the animal depicted on each ruler’s coins.

61.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Harishena — minister of Chandragupta II responsible for Udayagiri conquests
61.x: Harishena was the court poet of Samudragupta and composed the Allahabad Prashasti. Virasena, not Harishena, was the minister associated with the Udayagiri inscription and conquests of Chandragupta II.
61.tq: Find the wrong person–office association among otherwise familiar Gupta court figures.

61.s: Which one of the following was associated with the court of Chandragupta II?
61.x: Vetala Bhatta was one of the noted scholars associated with the Navaratnas of Chandragupta II’s court.
61.tq: Distinguish members of Chandragupta II’s court from inscription composers and feudatories.

61.s:
Assertion (A): Chandragupta II’s influence extended into the Deccan without direct annexation of the entire region.
Reason (R): His daughter Prabhavati Gupta married the Vakataka ruler Rudrasena II.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
61.x: Both statements are true, and the marriage of Prabhavati Gupta with Rudrasena II created an alliance through which Gupta influence extended into the Deccan.
61.tq: Check whether the stated marriage alliance directly explains the political consequence.

61.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the first Gupta ruler to assume the title of Maharajadhiraja?
61.x: Chandragupta I was the first Gupta ruler to assume the title of Maharajadhiraja.
61.tq: Identify the first holder of an imperial title rather than the most powerful ruler of the dynasty.

61.s: The Gupta Era is generally regarded as having begun in
61.x: The Gupta Era began in 319–320 CE.
61.tq: Distinguish the beginning of the era from the approximate reign dates of individual Gupta rulers.

61.s: Which one of the following best describes the extent of Samudragupta’s empire and influence?
o: It extended from Nepal and Punjab to Kanchi, with influence reaching Simhala.
It was confined to Magadha and the middle Ganga valley.
It extended only from Gujarat to western Malwa.
It covered the whole of the Deccan but excluded northern India.
61.x: Samudragupta’s empire extended from Nepal and Punjab to Kanchi, while his influence reached Simhala.
61.tq: Use the northern and southern limits together to identify the complete territorial description.

61.s:
Which of the following places were included among the targets of Samudragupta’s southern campaign in coastal Andhra?
1. Pishtapura
2. Vengi
3. Avamukta
4. Devarashtra
5. Erandapalle
6. Palakka
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
61.x: All six places—Pishtapura, Vengi, Avamukta, Devarashtra, Erandapalle and Palakka—are listed in connection with Samudragupta’s southern campaign in coastal Andhra.
61.tq: Test completeness of a named regional list; one omitted item makes a combination incorrect.

61.s: Hastivarman, mentioned in connection with Samudragupta’s southern campaign, was the ruler of
61.x: Hastivarman was the ruler of Vengi and belonged to the Salankayana line.
61.tq: Match the individual ruler with the specific Andhra centre in the campaign list.

61.s: The Allahabad Pillar inscription is particularly important for the history of fourth-century Andhra because it provides information about the kings of
61.x: The inscription is a chief source for information about the fourth-century Andhra regions and rulers of Vengi, Pishtapura, Avamukta and Devarashtra.
61.tq: Apply the source–region connection instead of selecting a better-known Gupta centre.

61.s: Which one of the following is the correct inscription–information combination?
o:
Allahabad Pillar — Samudragupta’s conquests
Bhitari — repulse of the Hunas

Mehrauli Iron Pillar — Mandsaur silk-weavers’ guild
Mandsaur — Chandragupta II’s Saka coins

Udayagiri — Bhanugupta’s earliest evidence of sati
Eran — Virasena’s record of conquests

Mehrauli Iron Pillar — Harishena’s Prayaga Prashasti
Allahabad Pillar — Skandagupta’s Huna victory
61.x: The Allahabad Pillar records Samudragupta’s conquests, while the Bhitari inscription records Skandagupta’s repulse of the Hunas. The other combinations interchange details belonging to different inscriptions.
61.tq: Separate closely related inscriptions by matching each with its distinctive historical content.

61.s: Samudragupta is regarded as the greatest Gupta ruler mainly because of his
o: extensive military conquests and wide political influence
establishment of Ujjain as the second capital
61.x: Samudragupta is regarded as the greatest Gupta ruler because of the extensive conquests and political influence described in the Allahabad Prashasti.
61.tq: Choose the broad historical significance rather than a specific achievement of another Gupta ruler.

62.s: Who is regarded as the founder of the Gupta dynasty and bore the title ‘Maharaja’?
62.x: Sri Gupta, who ruled approximately from 240 to 280 CE, is regarded as the founder of the Gupta dynasty and bore the title ‘Maharaja’.
62.tq: Use direct founder–title recall.

62.s: Ghatotkacha ruled approximately during which period?
62.x: Ghatotkacha ruled approximately from 280 to 319 CE, succeeding Sri Gupta.
62.tq: Distinguish adjacent Gupta reign periods through numerical recall.

62.s: The Gupta Era is generally associated with the accession of which ruler and the year 319–320 CE?
62.x: Chandragupta I ruled approximately from 319 to 335 CE, and the Gupta Era is associated with 319–320 CE.
62.tq: Link a historical era with its ruler and date.

62.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
62.x: Chandragupta I ruled approximately from 319 to 335 CE. The period c. 335–375 CE belongs to Samudragupta.
62.tq: Find the reversed adjacent reign period.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about the later Gupta rulers:
1. Vishnugupta was the last ruler of the main Gupta line.
2. Vishnugupta ruled approximately from 540 to 550 CE.
3. Purugupta, Kumaragupta II, Budhagupta, Narasimhagupta and Kumaragupta III belonged to the later Gupta succession.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: All three statements are correct. Vishnugupta was the last ruler of the main line and ruled approximately from 540 to 550 CE; the other named rulers belonged to the later Gupta succession.
62.tq: Check the ruler list, terminal ruler and date together.

62.s: Which of the following titles was borne by Chandragupta II?
62.x: Chandragupta II bore the title Vikramaditya. He was also known by the title Simhavikrama.
62.tq: Use direct ruler–title identification.

62.s:
Chandragupta II was also known by which of the following names?
1. Devagupta
2. Devaraja
3. Baladitya
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: Chandragupta II was also known as Devagupta and Devaraja. Baladitya was associated with Narasimhagupta, not Chandragupta II.
62.tq: Separate alternative names from names of other Gupta rulers.

62.s: The title ‘Simhavikrama’ of Chandragupta II is particularly associated with which type of coin?
62.x: Chandragupta II issued lion-slayer coins and used the title Simhavikrama. His father is associated with tiger-slayer coins.
62.tq: Discriminate between the lion-slayer and tiger-slayer coin types.

62.s: Which ruler was defeated by Chandragupta II in the Saka conquest?
62.x: Chandragupta II defeated Rudrasimha III and annexed western Malwa and Gujarat.
62.tq: Use the ruler–conquest association.

62.s: Which of the following regions were annexed by Chandragupta II after his Saka conquest?
62.x: Chandragupta II annexed western Malwa and Gujarat after defeating Rudrasimha III.
62.tq: Match the conquest with its territorial result.

62.s: The Udayagiri cave inscription recording the Saka campaign of Chandragupta II is associated with which person?
62.x: The Udayagiri cave inscription of Virasena records the campaign of Chandragupta II against the Sakas.
62.tq: Use inscription–author association rather than ruler recall alone.

62.s: Which inscription claims the extension of Chandragupta II’s authority towards north-western India and Bengal?
62.x: The Mehrauli iron pillar inscription claims Chandragupta II’s achievements in north-western India and Bengal.
62.tq: Distinguish inscriptions by the geographical claim they make.

62.s: Why are the silver coins of Chandragupta II regarded as strong evidence of his victory over the Sakas?
o: They were issued exclusively in western Malwa before the conquest.
They imitated Saka silver coins and were issued after the conquest.
They carried the portrait of Rudrasimha III.
They were the first Gupta coins issued in gold.
62.x: The silver coins of Chandragupta II were modelled on Saka silver coins and were issued after the Saka conquest, making them strong evidence of that victory.
62.tq: Infer historical evidence from the design, timing and material of coins.

62.s: The Saka-model silver coins of Chandragupta II weighed approximately:
62.x: The Saka-model silver coins of Chandragupta II weighed approximately 33 grains.
62.tq: Test the precise quantitative detail with close numerical distractors.

62.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Alliance)
A. Naga
B. Vakataka
C. Dhruvadevi

List-II (Detail)
1. Prabhavati married Rudrasena II
2. Marriage after the killing of Ramagupta
3. Marriage with Kuberanaga

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: Chandragupta II married Kuberanaga, a Naga princess; his daughter Prabhavati married Vakataka ruler Rudrasena II; Dhruvadevi was married after Ramagupta’s killing.
62.tq: Start from the sure alliance–marriage pair and eliminate the codes.

62.s: What was the political significance of Prabhavati Gupta’s marriage to Rudrasena II?
o: It led to the direct annexation of Magadha by the Vakatakas.
It established Ujjain as the Vakataka capital.
It enabled indirect Gupta control over the Vakataka kingdom.
It ended Gupta control over western Malwa.
62.x: Prabhavati Gupta’s marriage to Vakataka ruler Rudrasena II enabled Chandragupta II to exercise indirect control over the Vakataka kingdom.
62.tq: Identify the political consequence of a matrimonial alliance.

62.s: Fa-Hien visited India approximately during which period?
62.x: Fa-Hien visited India approximately from 399 to 414 CE, during the reign of Chandragupta II.
62.tq: Distinguish the pilgrim’s travel period from neighbouring Gupta reigns.

62.s: Which statement regarding Fa-Hien’s account is correct?
o: He explicitly named Chandragupta II as the reigning king in every account.
He visited India during the reign of Skandagupta to study military administration.
He did not name the king because his principal concern was Buddhism.
He was a Gupta court official appointed at Ujjain.
62.x: Fa-Hien was a Buddhist pilgrim, and he did not name the reigning king because his focus was Buddhism rather than political history.
62.tq: Reject the tempting but unsupported courtier and ruler-identification claims.

62.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the traditional Navaratnas of Chandragupta II?
62.x: Fa-Hien was a visiting Buddhist pilgrim, not one of the traditional Navaratnas. Kalidasa, Amarasimha and Varahamihira are included in the traditional list.
62.tq: Find the outsider in a well-known named list.

62.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the traditional Navaratnas of Chandragupta II?
1. Kalidasa — Navaratna
2. Dhanvantari — Navaratna
3. Kshapanaka — Navaratna
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: Kalidasa, Dhanvantari and Kshapanaka are all included in the traditional list of nine gems. The full list also includes Amarasimha, Varahamihira, Vararuchi, Shanku, Ghatakarpara and Vetalabhatta.
62.tq: Verify multiple members of a named traditional list.

62.s: The first Huna attack on the Gupta Empire occurred during the reign of:
62.x: The first Huna attack occurred during the reign of Kumaragupta I. It was repulsed by Prince Skandagupta.
62.tq: Separate the Gupta ruler during the first attack from the ruler who repelled it.

62.s: Who repelled the first Huna attack on the Gupta Empire?
62.x: Prince Skandagupta repelled the first Huna attack, which took place during the reign of Kumaragupta I.
62.tq: Discriminate between the attacked ruler and the military defender.

62.s: The Hunas who entered India in the mid-fifth century were also known as:
62.x: The Hunas were Hephthalites, also called White Huns. They came from Central Asia through the Oxus valley.
62.tq: Distinguish closely associated Central Asian peoples by their alternative names.

62.s: The initial route and early area of Huna expansion in India were respectively:
62.x: The Hephthalite or White Huns entered from Central Asia through the Oxus valley and occupied Gandhara.
62.tq: Match the invasion route with the first occupied region.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about Skandagupta’s Huna campaigns:
1. He repulsed the Hunas twice.
2. He assumed the title Vikramaditya after his victories.
3. His campaigns belonged to the reign of Kumaragupta I alone.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: Skandagupta repulsed the Hunas twice and took the title Vikramaditya. The later Huna waves occurred during his own reign, so statement 3 is false.
62.tq: Detect the statement that improperly confines a continuing invasion to one reign.

62.s: Which sequence correctly represents the Huna leaders and the Indian rulers associated with their defeat?
o: Toramana—no defeat stated; Mihirakula—Yashodharman and Narasimhagupta Baladitya
62.x: Toramana occupied large parts of western and central India, while Mihirakula was defeated by Yashodharman, Narasimhagupta Baladitya and the Maukharis.
62.tq: Separate the territorial advance of Toramana from the recorded defeat of Mihirakula.

62.s:
By approximately 485 CE, which of the following areas were held by the Hunas?
1. Punjab
2. Rajasthan
3. Kashmir
4. Eastern Malwa and central India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: By 485 CE, the Hunas held Punjab, Rajasthan, Kashmir, eastern Malwa and central India.
62.tq: Test the complete territorial extent rather than one isolated region.

62.s: Which statement about Mihirakula is correct?
o: He was defeated by Rudrasimha III in western Malwa.
He was the father of Toramana and patronised Buddhism.
He led the first Huna attack during Kumaragupta I’s reign.
He was the son of Toramana and persecuted Buddhists.
62.x: Mihirakula was the son of Toramana. He was described as a tyrant and iconoclast who persecuted Buddhists.
62.tq: Use the father–son relationship and religious policy as distinguishing clues.

62.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
A. First Huna attack
B. Later Huna waves
C. Toramana
D. Mihirakula

List-II
1. Narasimhagupta’s reign
2. Late Kumaragupta I’s reign
3. Skandagupta’s reign
4. Budhagupta and after

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: The first attack occurred during late Kumaragupta I; later waves during Skandagupta; Toramana advanced under Budhagupta and after; Mihirakula is associated with Narasimhagupta’s reign.
62.tq: Start with the fixed first-attack and later-wave pairs.

62.s: Skandagupta faced which two major threats during his reign?
62.x: Skandagupta faced the Pushyamitras, particularly at the end of Kumaragupta’s reign, and the Hunas during his own reign.
62.tq: Identify the exact pair of invasions faced by a ruler.

62.s: The Bhitari pillar inscription of Skandagupta is located in present-day:
62.x: The Bhitari pillar is located at Ghazipur in Uttar Pradesh and records Skandagupta’s victories over the Pushyamitras and Hunas.
62.tq: Match an inscription with its location and content.

62.s: Which inscription records the repair of the Sudarshana lake by Parnadatta, the governor of Skandagupta?
62.x: The Junagadh, or Girnar, inscription records that Parnadatta repaired the Sudarshana lake while serving as Skandagupta’s governor.
62.tq: Use the public-works detail to identify the correct inscription.

62.s: Which of the following features is depicted on Skandagupta’s gold coins?
o: A ship, a wheel and a seated Buddha
A tiger, a horse and a sacrificial altar
A bow and arrow, the Garuda standard and Lakshmi
A lion, a trident and Nandi
62.x: Skandagupta’s gold coins depict him with a bow and arrow, the Garuda standard and Lakshmi.
62.tq: Recall the distinctive iconography of a ruler’s coinage.

62.s: Which institutional change is associated with Skandagupta’s reign?
o: Governors became hereditary feudatories as central control weakened.
The Gupta Empire became a federation of independent republics immediately.
Provincial offices were transferred exclusively to Buddhist monasteries.
Governors were abolished and all provinces were directly administered from Pataliputra.
62.x: Central control weakened under Skandagupta, and governors increasingly became hereditary feudatories.
62.tq: Infer administrative decentralisation from the change in provincial offices.

62.s: The account of the Ramagupta episode is found in which work by Vishakhadatta?
62.x: The Ramagupta episode is narrated in Devichandraguptam, attributed to Vishakhadatta.
62.tq: Match the historical episode with its literary source.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about the Ramagupta episode:
1. Ramagupta was the elder brother of Chandragupta II.
2. Ramagupta agreed to surrender Dhruvadevi to a Saka king.
3. Chandragupta II killed the Saka king, subsequently killed Ramagupta and married Dhruvadevi.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: All three statements describe the traditional Ramagupta episode: the elder brother agreed to surrender Dhruvadevi, after which Chandragupta II killed the Saka king, killed Ramagupta and married Dhruvadevi.
62.tq: Test the succession dispute as a connected sequence of events.

62.s:
Arrange the following events in the correct chronological order:
A. First Huna attack during the reign of Kumaragupta I
B. Saka conquest by Chandragupta II
C. Later Huna waves during the reign of Skandagupta
D. Advance of Toramana into western and central India

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: The Saka conquest of Chandragupta II preceded the first Huna attack in late Kumaragupta I’s reign; later Huna waves occurred under Skandagupta, followed by Toramana’s advance under the weaker successors.
62.tq: Use the Gupta succession as the first framework, then place the invasions.

62.s: Which one of the following successor powers was associated with Magadha?
62.x: The Later Guptas established themselves in Magadha. The Maitrakas were associated with Valabhi, the Pushyabhutis with Thanesar and Kannauj, and the Aulikaras with Mandsaur.
62.tq: Use direct region–power association and eliminate neighbouring successor kingdoms.

62.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Maukharis — Bihar and Uttar Pradesh
2. Maitrakas — Gujarat and western Malwa
3. Pushyabhutis — Thanesar and later Kannauj
4. Aulikaras — Mandsaur and Malwa
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
62.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. The Maukharis were associated with Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, the Maitrakas with Gujarat and western Malwa, the Pushyabhutis with Thanesar and Kannauj, and the Aulikaras with Mandsaur and Malwa.
62.tq: Check each region–dynasty pair independently before selecting the coded combination.

62.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Power)
 a. Later Guptas
 b. Maitrakas
 c. Pushyabhutis
 d. Aulikaras

List-II (Centre or region)
 i. Mandsaur
 ii. Magadha
 iii. Valabhi
 iv. Thanesar and later Kannauj

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
62.x: The Later Guptas were associated with Magadha, the Maitrakas with Valabhi, the Pushyabhutis with Thanesar and later Kannauj, and the Aulikaras with Mandsaur.
62.tq: Start with the sure pair of a dynasty and its principal centre, then complete the code.

62.s: Which one of the following was NOT a power included among the major successor powers of the Guptas in the north and west?
62.x: The Paramaras of Malwa were a later power and were not included among the successor powers listed in this context. The Maukharis, Maitrakas and Pushyabhutis were included.
62.tq: Find the later dynasty that does not belong to the contemporary successor group.

62.s: The Mandsaur prashasti of the silk weavers' guild and the Mandsaur pillar inscriptions of Yashodharman are associated with which regional power?
62.x: Both groups of inscriptions come from the Aulikara area centred on Mandsaur in Malwa. They represent different aspects of the political and social history of that region.
62.tq: Link two inscriptional references through their common regional setting.

62.s:
Which one of the following combinations is correct regarding the regional powers mentioned in the post-Gupta period?
1. Guptas — Magadha
2. Pushyabhutis — Thanesar
3. Maukharis — Kannauj
4. Maitrakas — Valabhi
62.x: All four combinations are correct. The Guptas of Magadha, Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, Maukharis of Kannauj and Maitrakas of Valabhi formed important regional powers after Gupta authority weakened.
62.tq: Test a compact set of dynasty–centre associations, including the easily confused centres of Thanesar and Kannauj.

62.s: Which of the following was an external factor contributing to the decline of the Gupta Empire?
o: Migration of silk weavers to Malwa
62.x: Repeated Huna invasions were an external cause of Gupta decline. The other factors represent economic or feudatory-related explanations.
62.tq: Classify the cause by distinguishing external pressure from internal administrative and economic causes.

62.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the causes of Gupta decline:
1. Land grants encouraged the growth of feudatories.
2. Hereditary governors strengthened the centralised control of the emperor.
3. The rise of Maukharis, Maitrakas, Later Guptas and Pushyabhutis weakened Gupta authority.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because hereditary governors contributed to the growth of autonomous feudatories rather than strengthening centralised imperial control.
62.tq: Spot the reversed effect in the statement about hereditary governors.

62.s:
Assertion (A): The Gupta state found it difficult to maintain a professional army in the later period.
Reason (R): Land grants reduced the revenue available to the state.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
62.x: Both statements are true, and the reduction of state revenue through land grants directly weakened the state's ability to maintain a professional army.
62.tq: Test a direct cause-and-effect relationship between declining revenue and military weakness.

62.s: Which one of the following best explains the economic impact of the loss of western India on the Gupta Empire?
o: It brought the western feudatories under tighter imperial control.
It enabled the state to maintain a larger professional army.
It increased the inflow of gold from western ports.
It reduced trade income, including income connected with Roman silk trade.
62.x: The loss of western India reduced trade income and contributed to the loss of revenue from the Roman silk trade. This aggravated the financial and military weakness of the empire.
62.tq: Apply the economic-cause chain from territorial loss to declining state revenue.

62.s: The migration of silk weavers from Gujarat to Malwa is dated to approximately:
62.x: The migration of silk weavers from Gujarat to Malwa is associated with AD 473. It is used as evidence of changing economic conditions during the Gupta period.
62.tq: Distinguish the economic date from the nearby inscriptional dates of 415, 510 and 532 CE.

62.s: Which one of the following was NOT identified as a cause of the decline of the Gupta Empire in the explanations listed?
62.x: The Arab invasion was not a cause of Gupta decline in this context. Huna invasions, the growth of feudatories and the loss of western trade revenue were identified causes.
62.tq: Use the explicit exception and separate a later invasion from the relevant Gupta-period causes.

62.s:
Which of the following combinations correctly explains the weakening of Gupta military power?
1. Huna invasions drained the treasury and army.
2. Falling trade revenue reduced state resources.
3. Land grants restricted the revenue available for maintaining troops.
4. Feudatories strengthened the emperor's direct control over the provinces.
62.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the growth of feudatories weakened direct imperial control rather than strengthening it.
62.tq: Combine military, fiscal and administrative causes while rejecting the reversed statement about feudatories.

62.s: Who was the last ruler of the Gupta Empire, with a reign generally placed around c. 540–550 CE?
62.x: Vishnugupta is identified as the last Gupta ruler, with his reign placed approximately between 540 and 550 CE.
62.tq: Use the terminal ruler and approximate reign dates as a direct chronology marker.

62.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the later Gupta period is correct?
o: The empire was strengthened by a succession of powerful rulers after Skandagupta.
The weakness of successors after Skandagupta contributed to imperial decline.
The loss of western India increased Gupta trade revenue.
The Gupta administration became more centralised than that of the Mauryas.
62.x: Weak successors after Skandagupta contributed to the decline of Gupta authority. The other statements reverse the recorded political and economic trends.
62.tq: Reject reversed comparisons and identify the correct succession-based explanation.

62.s:
Which titles were associated with Kumaragupta I?
1. Shakraditya
2. Mahendraditya
3. Vikramaditya
4. Devanampriya
62.x: Kumaragupta I was associated with the titles Shakraditya and Mahendraditya. Vikramaditya is associated in this context with Chandragupta II and Skandagupta, while Devanampriya is not listed for Kumaragupta I.
62.tq: Discriminate between similar royal titles belonging to different rulers.

62.s: Kumaragupta I is traditionally associated with the foundation of which institution?
62.x: Kumaragupta I is associated with the foundation of Nalanda University. The other institutions are not identified here as his foundation.
62.tq: Test the ruler–institution association directly.

62.s:
Which of the following statements about Kumaragupta I is/are correct?
1. He was a devotee of Kartikeya.
2. He performed an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
3. He issued new gold coin types depicting Kartikeya.
4. He faced the Pushyamitras and the first Huna attack late in his reign.
62.x: All four statements are correct. Kumaragupta I was associated with Kartikeya worship, performed an Ashvamedha, issued relevant gold coin types and faced the Pushyamitras and the first Huna attack.
62.tq: Use a multi-fact ruler profile and verify each statement before choosing the complete combination.

62.s: A gold coin shows a Gupta ruler feeding a peacock, with Kartikeya also represented. Such a coin type is associated with:
62.x: Kumaragupta I issued new gold coin types showing Kartikeya and the king feeding a peacock. This imagery reflects his association with Kartikeya.
62.tq: Identify the ruler from distinctive coin imagery rather than from a title alone.

62.s: Which inscription is regarded as the earliest inscription of Kumaragupta I and is dated to Gupta year 96, corresponding to 415 CE?
62.x: The Bilsad inscription is regarded as Kumaragupta I's earliest inscription. Gupta year 96 corresponds to 415 CE in this record.
62.tq: Match the earliest inscription with its ruler and convert the regnal year to the stated CE date.

62.s:
Which of the following inscriptions or records is correctly associated with Kumaragupta I?
1. Bilsad inscription
2. Karandanda inscription
3. Mandsor inscription
4. Damodarpur copper plates
62.x: All four are associated with Kumaragupta I. The Damodarpur copper plates are also notable for indicating guilds acting as banks.
62.tq: Test the completeness of an inscription list through coded combinations.

62.s: The Damodarpur copper plates provide evidence that guilds in the Gupta period could function as:
62.x: The Damodarpur copper plates indicate that guilds could act as banks. This illustrates their important economic role in the Gupta period.
62.tq: Identify the institutional function from an inscriptional reference.

62.s: Yashodharman, who rose in Malwa, was originally a:
62.x: Yashodharman was a Gupta feudatory in Malwa. His subsequent rise and victory over Mihirakula further undermined Gupta authority.
62.tq: Use the political relationship between a regional ruler and the Gupta centre as the discriminator.

62.s: Yashodharman's victory pillars at Sondani near Mandasor are generally dated to approximately:
62.x: Yashodharman's victory pillars at Sondani are dated to approximately 532 CE. They commemorate his victory over Mihirakula.
62.tq: Separate the date of Yashodharman's victory from the earlier Bilsad, silk-weaver and Eran dates.

62.s: Which inference most accurately follows from Yashodharman's victory over Mihirakula?
o: It brought Malwa permanently under direct Gupta administration.
It demonstrated the rise of a regional power and further weakened Gupta authority.
It ended the process of regionalisation in northern India.
It immediately restored the Gupta Empire to its former extent.
62.x: Yashodharman's victory did not revive the Gupta Empire; his own rise as a regional power undermined Gupta authority and reflected the wider process of political fragmentation.
62.tq: Distinguish the immediate military success from its broader political consequence.

62.s: The Eran boar inscription is significant because it records:
o: Huna rule over Eran in the first regnal year of Toramana
The victory of Yashodharman over Mihirakula
The migration of silk weavers from Gujarat to Malwa
The foundation of Nalanda by Kumaragupta I
62.x: The Eran boar inscription was built in Toramana's first regnal year and records Huna rule over Eran.
62.tq: Link a monument with the exact Huna ruler and political circumstance named in the record.

62.s: The Eran inscription dated to 510 CE is associated with which event?
o: The defeat of Mihirakula by Yashodharman
The first Huna attack during Kumaragupta's reign
The sati of Goparaja, the general of Bhanugupta
62.x: The 510 CE Eran inscription records the sati of Goparaja, who was the general of Bhanugupta, and is regarded as the earliest sati record in this context.
62.tq: Use the date and named individuals to distinguish two different Eran records.

62.s: Which literary work, apart from inscriptions, mentions the Hunas?
62.x: Banabhatta's Harshacharita also mentions the Hunas. The other works are not identified here as the relevant literary reference.
62.tq: Match the historical group with the literary source that mentions it.

62.s: The absence of Gupta coins and inscriptions in western Malwa and Saurashtra after the reign of Skandagupta indicates:
o: The complete end of trade in eastern India
Expansion of Gupta control into western India
Loss of Gupta control over those territories
62.x: The absence of Gupta coins and inscriptions after Skandagupta in western Malwa and Saurashtra is evidence that these areas were no longer under effective Gupta control.
62.tq: Infer territorial change from the geographic distribution of material evidence.

62.s: Which regional dynasty is correctly matched with its political and cultural profile?
o: Maitrakas — Banavasi; Rudrasena II patronised Ajanta
Vishnukundins — Gujarat; Madhava Varma II ruled Valabhi
Vakatakas — Vidarbha and northern Maharashtra; Harishena patronised Ajanta
62.x: The Vakatakas were associated with northern Maharashtra and Vidarbha, and Harishena patronised Ajanta. The other options incorrectly combine dynasties, regions and personalities.
62.tq: Use the dynasty–region–patron combination and detect swapped rulers or centres.

62.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Vakatakas:
1. They were Brahmins.
2. They succeeded the Satavahanas in their region.
3. They were contemporaries of the Guptas.
4. Rudrasena II married Prabhavati Gupta.
62.x: All four statements are correct. The Vakatakas were Brahmins, successors of the Satavahanas, contemporaries of the Guptas, and Rudrasena II married Prabhavati Gupta.
62.tq: Verify a complete dynasty profile instead of relying on one famous association.

62.s: The Kadambas of Banavasi were founded by:
62.x: Mayurasharma founded the Kadamba dynasty of Banavasi in Karnataka.
62.tq: Test the founder–dynasty association directly, a common historical trap.

62.s:
Which of the following statements about Madhava Varma II is correct?
1. He was a ruler of the Vishnukundins.
2. He ruled approximately from 440 to 495 CE.
3. He won over 100 battles.
4. He performed 11 Ashvamedhas.
62.x: All four statements are correct. Madhava Varma II was the greatest Vishnukundin ruler, ruled around 440–495 CE, won over 100 battles and performed 11 Ashvamedhas.
62.tq: Combine ruler, dates, military achievement and ritual achievement in one coded question.

62.s: Which inscription records the defeat of Indrabhattaraka Varma by the Maukhari ruler Ishanavarma?
62.x: The Jaunpur inscription of Uttar Pradesh records the defeat of Indrabhattaraka Varma by the Maukhari ruler Ishanavarma.
62.tq: Match the political event with the specific inscription and location.

62.s: The clash between the Vishnukundins and the Maukharis is significant for Andhra history because it:
o: Links Andhra political developments with North Indian regional politics.
Proves that the Maukharis ruled the whole of coastal Andhra.
Marks the beginning of the Satavahana period.
Shows that the Vishnukundins founded the Gupta Empire.
62.x: The Vishnukundin–Maukhari conflict links Andhra history with the political struggles among northern Indian regional powers in the post-Gupta period.
62.tq: Apply a regional-history fact to its wider political significance.

62.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Kumaragupta I's Bilsad inscription
B. Migration of silk weavers from Gujarat to Malwa
C. Eran inscription of Bhanugupta's general Goparaja
D. Yashodharman's victory pillars at Sondani
62.x: The correct sequence is 415 CE, 473 CE, 510 CE and approximately 532 CE. These correspond respectively to the Bilsad inscription, silk-weaver migration, the Eran record and Yashodharman's victory pillars.
62.tq: Fix the earliest and latest dates first, then place the two middle events.

62.s: Which statement best expresses the historical significance of the Gupta decline?
o: It marked the transition from a single empire towards regional kingdoms and a feudal order.
It ended the emergence of all regional dynasties in northern India.
It converted all land grants into direct imperial taxation.
It resulted in the permanent restoration of Mauryan centralisation.
62.x: The break-up of Gupta authority marked a movement from a single empire to regional kingdoms and a more feudal political order.
62.tq: Identify the broad historical consequence without being misled by absolute alternatives.

62.s: The title 'Vikramaditya' was used by which pair of Gupta rulers?
62.x: The title Vikramaditya was used by both Chandragupta II and Skandagupta. When a question asks for the principal Gupta ruler associated with Vikramaditya, it commonly refers to Chandragupta II, but both rulers used the title.
62.tq: Separate a shared title from the ruler most commonly associated with it.

62.s: Which comparison is correctly stated regarding the decline of the Guptas and the Kushans?
o: The Guptas and Kushans both retained uninterrupted imperial control after regional powers rose.
The Kushans expanded after the Sasanians defeated them.
Only the Guptas faced external pressure; the Kushans declined solely because of trade.
Both faced external pressure along with the rise of an Indian power.
62.x: The Kushans declined under pressure from the Sasanians together with the rise of an Indian power, while the Guptas similarly faced external invasions and the rise of regional powers.
62.tq: Compare the common structural pattern rather than matching only one dynasty-specific event.

62.s:
Which of the following developments most clearly illustrates the shift from imperial administration to a feudatory order after the Guptas?
1. Hereditary governors became important local powers.
2. Land beneficiaries acquired greater autonomy.
3. Regional powers such as Yashodharman, the Maukharis and the Maitrakas rose.
4. Provincial authorities became entirely dependent on direct imperial appointment.
62.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 correctly describe the growth of feudatory and regional power. Statement 4 is false because provincial authorities became less dependent on direct imperial control.
62.tq: Recognise the institutional pattern of decentralisation and reject the reversed statement.

63.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Grant)
a. Brahmadeya
b. Agrahara
c. Devagrahara

d. Secular grant

List-II (Grantee)
i. Officials or feudatories
 ii. Temples and monasteries
 iii. Brahmanas, individually or collectively
 iv. Brahmanas as religious functionaries

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
63.x: Brahmadeya was granted to Brahmanas singly or collectively, agrahara was tax-free land or a village given to Brahmanas, devagrahara was assigned to temples and monasteries, and secular grants went to officials or feudatories in lieu of salary.
63.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes containing a swapped grantee.

63.s: Which one of the following best describes the rights commonly transferred along with a land grant during the Gupta and post-Gupta period?
o: Revenue-collecting, administrative, judicial and police rights
Only the right to collect customs duties at ports
Exclusive control over the royal army
Only the right to cultivate the land
63.x: Land grants often transferred revenue as well as administrative, judicial and police rights to the grantees. Royal officials could consequently be barred from entering the granted area.
63.tq: Who would exercise the associated administrative and judicial powers?

63.s:
Consider the following statements regarding land grants in tribal and forest regions:
1. They brought virgin land under cultivation.
2. They contributed to the absorption of tribal groups into the caste order.
3. The absorbed tribal groups could emerge as new sub-castes.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Land grants in tribal and forest frontiers brought virgin land under cultivation and integrated tribal communities into the caste order, where they could appear as new sub-castes.
63.tq: Test the full chain of cause, social effect and resulting classification.

63.s: Which of the following was a consequence of the expansion of land grants for the peasantry?
o: Peasants became hereditary feudatories of the king
Peasants acquired complete freedom from taxes and labour obligations
Peasants were converted exclusively into urban merchants
Peasants were reduced to semi-servile conditions, including tenancy and forced labour
63.x: The expansion of grants reduced many peasants to semi-servile status. Tenant farming, sharecropping, tenants-at-will and forced labour were associated with this process.
63.tq: Use the social consequence rather than the grant category to identify the answer.

63.s: The earliest land grants in India are associated with which dynasty?
63.x: The Satavahanas are associated with the earliest land grants in India.
63.tq: Direct dynasty–institution recall with nearby-period distractors.

63.s:
Match the following tenures with their descriptions:

a. Nivi dharma
b. Nivi dharma akshayana
c. Aprada dharma
d. Bhumichchhidranyaya

i. Enjoyment of income without the right of alienation
 ii. Perpetual endowment
 iii. Trust
 iv. Ownership by the first reclaimer of waste land

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
63.x: Nivi dharma meant a trust, nivi dharma akshayana a perpetual endowment, aprada dharma enjoyment of income without alienation, and bhumichchhidranyaya ownership by the first reclaimer of waste land.
63.tq: Match each technical tenure with its distinctive legal consequence.

63.s: Which of the following statements about granted villages is NOT correct?
o: Royal officials were often barred from entering the granted area.
The grantees could receive the revenue from the land.
The grant necessarily abolished all forms of local authority and produced direct royal administration.
Administrative, judicial and police rights could accompany the grant.
63.x: Grants tended to remove or restrict direct royal intervention rather than produce direct royal administration. The grantees could receive revenue and administrative, judicial and police rights, while royal officials were often barred from entry.
63.tq: Find the statement that reverses the effect of delegated rights.

63.s: The grant of 100 nivartanas to Buddhist monks and agrahara-type grants to Brahmanas are associated with which dynasty?
63.x: The Satavahana period provides the precedent of granting 100 nivartanas to Buddhist monks and making agrahara-type grants to Brahmanas.
63.tq: Link the numerical land grant with its dynasty and beneficiaries.

63.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Devadana — revenue assignment to feudatories in lieu of salary
Brahmadeya — grant to temples exclusively for worship
Agrahara — tax-free, often hereditary grant to Brahmanas
Secular grant — land assigned only to Buddhist monks
63.x: An agrahara was a tax-free, often hereditary grant to Brahmanas and could include administrative rights. Devadana or devagrahara was associated with temples and monasteries, while secular grants could go to officials or feudatories.
63.tq: Reject swapped beneficiaries by identifying the exact grant–recipient relationship.

63.s: In the context of ancient Indian revenue terminology, ‘bhaga’ referred to:
o: Periodic supplies of fruits and firewood
The king’s share of agricultural produce
63.x: Bhaga was the king’s share of agricultural produce and constituted the principal land revenue.
63.tq: Distinguish the principal produce share from in-kind supplies and labour obligations.

63.s: Which of the following correctly describes ‘bhoga’ in the Gupta-period revenue system?
o: A tax on the sale and purchase of land
Periodic supplies such as fruits, firewood and flowers to the king
63.x: Bhoga consisted of periodic supplies in kind, including fruits, firewood and flowers, made to the king.
63.tq: Separate periodic in-kind supplies from cash and land-related taxes.

63.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Udranga was an additional or new tax.
2. Uparikara was probably imposed on temporary tenants.
3. Udakabhaga denoted a water tax.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Udranga and uparikara were additional or new taxes, with uparikara probably associated with temporary tenants. Udakabhaga referred to a water tax.
63.tq: Combine closely related tax terms and eliminate the code containing a reversed meaning.

63.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Sulka — forced labour for the army
Bali — initially voluntary and later compulsory
63.x: Sulka was a customs duty or toll. Forced labour for the army and officials was called vishti; hiranya was a cash tax, bali changed from voluntary to compulsory, and kara was a periodic tax.
63.tq: Identify the deliberately swapped meaning among neighbouring revenue terms.

63.s: The term ‘halivakara’ denoted:
63.x: Halivakara was the tax imposed on the plough.
63.tq: Use the occupational clue in the term while separating it from other tax categories.

63.s: Vishti in the agrarian and revenue context refers to:
o: Forced labour rendered for the army and officials
A tax on the purchase of land
63.x: Vishti was forced labour exacted for the needs of the army and officials.
63.tq: Discriminate a labour obligation from taxes and land measures.

63.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies ‘aprahata’?
63.x: Aprahata referred to uncultivated forest land.
63.tq: Distinguish the specific forest-land term from the broader categories of waste and habitable land.

63.s: Kuliyavapa and dronavapa were used as terms for:
63.x: Kuliyavapa and dronavapa denoted measures of land.
63.tq: Test the paired terms together so that a tax term is not confused with a measurement term.

63.s:
Match the land categories with their meanings:

a. Kshetra
b. Khila
c. Vastu

i. Habitable land
 ii. Cultivable land
 iii. Waste land

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
63.x: Kshetra meant cultivable land, khila meant waste land, and vastu meant habitable land.
63.tq: Start with the familiar cultivable-land term and complete the classification by elimination.

63.s: Klipta and upaklipta were associated with which type of levy?
o: Customs duties on overseas trade only
Payments made in kind to temples
Taxes on the produce of forest land
Taxes on the sale and purchase of land
63.x: Klipta and upaklipta referred to taxes connected with the sale and purchase of land.
63.tq: Match the paired technical terms with the transaction to which they relate.

63.s: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the variation in the prescribed land-revenue share found in different sources?
o: The law books prescribe one-seventh and all other sources prescribe one-sixth.
All sources uniformly prescribe one-half of the produce.
The law books prescribe one-sixth, while other references mention one-seventh or a range of one-fourth to one-sixth.
No source gives a proportionate share of agricultural produce.
63.x: The law books prescribe one-sixth, while different references mention one-seventh or a range from one-fourth to one-sixth. This variation should be distinguished from the standard law-book prescription.
63.tq: Compare the competing figures instead of treating one reported rate as universal.

63.s: Which of the following trends in taxation is associated with the period under consideration?
o: Land taxes rose while trade taxes fell
Land taxes fell while trade taxes rose
Both land taxes and trade taxes disappeared
Both land taxes and trade taxes rose at the same rate
63.x: The broad trend was an increase in land taxes accompanied by a decline in trade taxes.
63.tq: Read the direction of both trends together and reject the reversed comparison.

63.s: Which historian associated Indian feudalism with land grants, sub-infeudation, vishti, decline of trade and urban decay?
63.x: R.S. Sharma argued that Indian feudalism crystallised through land grants, sub-infeudation, vishti, decline of trade and urban decay.
63.tq: Use the historian–argument association directly.

63.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: D.C. Sircar — Grants transferred revenue rights rather than ownership
Harbans Mukhia — Existence of widespread serfdom in India
B.D. Chattopadhyaya — Integrative and processual model
R.S. Sharma — Land grants and urban decay as elements of Indian feudalism
63.x: Harbans Mukhia argued that there was no serfdom and that Indian peasants were largely free and retained autonomy.
63.tq: Find the swapped or opposite interpretation in a historian–position pair.

63.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the interpretation of Indian feudalism:
1. D.C. Sircar held that land grants transferred revenue rights, not ownership.
2. Harbans Mukhia emphasised the absence of serfdom and the existence of a largely free peasantry.
3. B.D. Chattopadhyaya regarded the spread of grants as a means of extending state society into new areas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: All three statements correctly represent the positions of D.C. Sircar, Harbans Mukhia and B.D. Chattopadhyaya respectively.
63.tq: Check each historian’s distinctive position before selecting the combined code.

63.s: Which of the following was cited as evidence for the emergence of Indian feudalism in the seventh century?
o: Expansion of long-distance trade and rapid urbanisation
Decline in long-distance trade and gold coinage
Opening of villages to unrestricted external trade
Increase in the circulation of gold coins
63.x: The evidence cited included the seventh-century decline in long-distance trade and gold coinage, shrinking towns and a closed village economy.
63.tq: Identify the option that preserves the stated historical trend rather than reversing it.

63.s: In the context of feudalism, which combination represents its essential elements?
o: Control and possession of land, lord–vassal relationship and weak central authority
Strong central authority, salaried bureaucracy and absence of land control
Popular sovereignty, elected local bodies and monetised taxation
Maritime trade, urban guilds and direct imperial administration
63.x: The essential elements are power based on control of land, lord–vassal ties and weak central authority. A strong centre with weak local authority is not a feudal feature.
63.tq: Separate the essential features from the deliberately reversed strong-centre description.

63.s: Under the stated definition of feudalism, an overlord granted land to a donee together with which rights?
o: Only the right to cultivate the land
Religious, educational and commercial rights בלבד
63.x: The defining grant involved fiscal, administrative and judicial rights in addition to the land itself.
63.tq: Recall the complete three-part rights combination attached to the grant.

63.s:
Arrange the following Gupta administrative units from the largest to the smallest:
A. Grama
B. Vithi
C. Bhukti
D. Vishaya
63.x: The correct descending order is Bhukti, Vishaya, Vithi and Grama.
63.tq: Use the administrative hierarchy from province to village.

63.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
63.x: The Vithi, particularly in eastern India, was associated with the Ayuktaka and other officials. A Bhukti was headed by an Uparika, a Vishaya by a Vishayapati, and a village by a Gramika or Gramadhyaksha.
63.tq: Start with the sure officer–unit pair and eliminate the swapped administrative levels.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about Gupta administrative units:
1. Bhukti could also be referred to as desha or rashtra.
2. Vishaya denoted a district and was headed by a Vishayapati.
3. Vithi represented a group of villages.
4. Grama was headed by a Gramika or Gramadhyaksha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: All four statements are correct. Bhukti was the provincial unit, Vishaya the district, Vithi a group of villages, and Grama the village unit.
63.tq: Verify the hierarchy and the officer attached to each level.

63.s: Which administrative practice indicates the participation of village authorities in land transactions during the Gupta period?
o: Consent of the village headman was required
Approval of the Sandhivigrahika was required
The town board alone authorised village transfers
Only the king could validate every transaction
63.x: The village headman’s consent was required for land transactions, indicating a role for local village authority.
63.tq: Apply the institutional fact to the land-transfer situation.

63.s: Which of the following statements regarding Gupta kingship is correct?
o: The title Maharajadhiraja was used exclusively by village headmen
Gupta kings used titles such as Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja and Paramabhattaraka
Gupta kings rejected all divine associations
Gupta rulers claimed that kingship was elective
63.x: Gupta rulers used the exalted titles Parameshvara, Maharajadhiraja and Paramabhattaraka and made divine claims about kingship.
63.tq: Recognise the cluster of royal titles rather than the absolute distractors.

63.s: Samudragupta was equated with which of the following deities or divine figures?
63.x: Samudragupta was equated with Kubera or Dhanada, Varuna, Indra and Yama or Antaka.
63.tq: Recall the complete set of divine comparisons associated with the ruler.

63.s: Which statement best describes succession and administration under the Gupta kings?
o: Kingship was hereditary, but primogeniture was not firmly established
Primogeniture was an inviolable constitutional rule
Kingship was transferred only through the feudatories
Kingship was elective and succession was determined by village councils
63.x: Gupta kingship was hereditary, but there was no firm rule of primogeniture. Several offices were also hereditary, and salaries were often paid in land or kind.
63.tq: Distinguish hereditary succession from the stronger and unsupported claim of fixed primogeniture.

63.s:
With reference to the Gupta Empire, consider the following statements:
1. It was less centralised than the Mauryan Empire.
2. Feudatories and land grantees administered substantial parts of the empire.
3. Some offices were hereditary.
4. Samudragupta reinstated some feudatories.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: All four statements are correct. Gupta administration relied substantially on feudatories and grantees, and it was considerably less centralised than Mauryan administration.
63.tq: Test the decentralisation pattern through several connected administrative features.

63.s: Which official was the Gupta minister of peace and war?
63.x: The Sandhivigrahika was the minister responsible for peace and war.
63.tq: Match the official with the specialised function.

63.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Pustapala — Minister of peace and war
Dutaka — Chief artisan of the town
63.x: The Dandapashika was the district police officer. The Mahadandanayaka was a chief judicial or military officer, the Pustapala kept land-transfer records, and the Dutaka acted as a spy or messenger.
63.tq: Use function-based elimination among officials with similar administrative roles.

63.s: The Kumaramatyas in the Gupta administration were best described as
o: foreign ambassadors appointed only during wartime
guild representatives responsible for town sanitation
village accountants with no access to higher offices
high-cadre officers from whom ministers and commanders could be selected
63.x: Kumaramatyas were senior or high-cadre officers, ranked with princes; ministers and commanders were chosen from them. They had their own office and were often paid in cash.
63.tq: Identify the broader cadre role instead of a narrow functional description.

63.s: Harisena is associated with the simultaneous holding of which offices?
63.x: Harisena held the offices of Kumaramatya, Sandhivigrahika and Mahadandanayaka together.
63.tq: Recall the distinctive three-office combination linked with Harisena.

63.s: Which official was responsible for keeping royal records, while the Pustapala maintained land-transfer records?
63.x: The Akshapataladhikrita kept royal records, whereas the Pustapala was the keeper of land-transfer records.
63.tq: Separate the two record-keeping offices by the type of record maintained.

63.s: Who represented the chief artisan community on the Gupta town board?
63.x: The Prathama kulika represented the chief artisans or craft guilds on the town board.
63.tq: Match the occupational representative with the social group represented.

63.s:
Consider the following pairs relating to the Gupta town board:
1. Nagarashreshthi — Chief banker or merchant
2. Sarthavaha — Chief caravan trader
3. Prathama kulika — Chief artisan
4. Prathama kayastha — Chief scribe
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
63.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. These representatives formed the town board, or adhikarana, with the Nagarashreshthi serving as its chairman.
63.tq: Verify every occupational representation before choosing the complete combination.

63.s: Which member of the Gupta town board served as its chairman?
63.x: The Nagarashreshthi, the chief banker or merchant, served as chairman of the town council or adhikarana.
63.tq: Distinguish the presiding member from the other professional representatives.

63.s: The Damodarpur copper plates are associated with which aspect of Gupta administration?
o: Description of a district council assisting an officer
Appointment of the Mauryan provincial governors
63.x: The Damodarpur copper plates describe a district council that assisted the concerned officer.
63.tq: Link the epigraphic source with the administrative institution it records.

63.s: In Gupta administrative terminology, the term ‘Kayastha’ primarily referred to
63.x: Kayasthas were associated with scribal and official work; the Prathama kayastha represented the chief scribes on the town board.
63.tq: Discriminate the exact occupational meaning of a familiar administrative term.

63.s: Which of the following sets contains only the law books associated with the Gupta period?
o: Narada, Brihaspati, Katyayana and Vishnu Smritis
Manusmriti, Arthashastra, Yajnavalkya Smriti and Rajatarangini
Katyayana, Panini, Charaka and Vishnu Smriti
63.x: Narada, Brihaspati, Katyayana and the Vishnu Smritis are identified as important law books of the period.
63.tq: Identify the complete list by eliminating authors and works from unrelated fields.

63.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the judicial system of the Gupta period:
1. Civil and criminal law were more clearly separated than in earlier periods.
2. Theft and adultery were treated as criminal offences.
